title: Behind the scenes of tidyverse development: new dplyr functions | Davis Vaughan | Data Science Lab
description:
The Data Science Lab is a live weekly call. Register at pos.it/dslab! Discord invites go out each week on lives calls. We'd love to have you! 

The Lab is an open, messy space for learning and asking questions. Think of it like pair coding with a friend or two. Learn something new, and share what you know to help others grow.

On this call, Libby Heeren is joined by Davis Vaughan, Positron and tidyverse dev, who walks through the newest functions in dplyr, the problems they solve, how decisions are made to add or replace functions, and how community-driven development drives the tidyverse (and how wife-driven development drives Davis!).

comments.text: Davis didn't talked about it, but i'm really confused of the purpose of when_all that was recently added. I mean, when_any is enough clear, you can essentially replace or statement (|) with commas, but when_all isn't just the same as using simply filter? filter(when_all(condition1, condition2, condition3)) isn't just the same as filter(condition1, condition2, condition3)?
comments.author: @letstalkaboutmath2121

comments.text: It's true that filter(when_all(condition1, condition2, condition3)) is the same as filter(condition1, condition2, condition3). But one thing to remember is that when_all() and when_any() aren't restricted to just being used inside of filter(). They are "normal" functions that can be used anywhere! Because of that, it makes sense to have both. when_all() is for when you need repeated & operations chained together, when_any()  is for when you need repeated | operations chained together. It just-so-happens to be the case that filter() + when_any() solve a really nice problem, but the tool is more generic than that!

comments.text:
Just FYI, the "lookup" package already has this recoding capability.

library(dplyr)

likert <- tibble(
  score = c(1,2,3,4,5,2,3,1,4)
)

lookuptab <- tribble(
  ~from, ~to,
  1, "Strong disagree",
  2, "Disagree",
  3, "Neutral",
  4, "Agree",
  5, "Strong agree"
  )

library(lookup)
likert |> mutate(category=lookup(score, lookuptab$from, lookuptab$to))
comments.author: @kevinwright9682

comments.text: Thanks! We know the community has tried to solve this in a number of ways. The dplyr solution has a number of additional benefits, including: the case_when style interface, the unmatched argument, a type-stable replace_values() variant, and support for a much wider array of types via being backed by the vctrs package.
comments.author: @PositPBC
